reality_anchor.topic: Why do lakes freeze from the top down instead of the bottom up?
evidence_claims: - The article states that liquid water can persist beneath thick ice at the ice–bedrock boundary because high pressure lowers the melting point of ice; overlying ice melts slowly and meltwater flows to low-pressure areas and pools to form subglacial lakes. - It reports that these lakes can remain isolated from the atmosphere for millions of years, with more than 400 identified under Antarctic and other ice sheets, and that Antarctic subglacial lakes alone may contain about 10,000 km³ of water, estimated as about 15% of Earth’s liquid freshwater.

- The authors report detecting 124 active subglacial lakes beneath the Antarctic ice sheet (north of 86° S) during 2003–08 using ICESat, with lakes filling and draining on months-to-years timescales. - They note these lakes are prevalent in coastal Antarctica, sometimes transfer water between one another, and often exchange water with distributed sources undetectable by ICESat. - They add that these reservoirs may contribute pulses of water that produce rapid temporal changes in glacier speeds, and may also withdraw water at other times to slow flow.
